title.en: Cells: hands-on activities from the textbook

text.en: A cell is too small to see with the eye, so scientists measure and observe it with a microscope. Chapter 2 gives five activities that let you measure a cell, watch water move through one and compare plant and animal cells.

Activity 2.1 estimates the size of a cell. First place a transparent millimetre ruler on the microscope stage and measure the diameter of the field of view. A 5 mm diameter is 5 x 1000 = 5000 micrometres.
Then replace the ruler with an onion peel, focus, and count how many cells lie along the diameter. Cell size is the field diameter divided by the number of cells.
Activity 2.2 uses two equal pieces of potato. Weigh both, put one in plain water and the other in a 20 per cent salt or sugar solution, and leave them for about an hour. Weigh again and compare.
The piece in plain water gains weight because water enters its cells, and the piece in the concentrated solution loses weight because water leaves. This movement of water through the cell membrane is osmosis.
Activity 2.3 compares cells. Make a temporary slide of an onion or Rhoeo leaf peel stained with safranin, and a slide of cheek cells stained with methylene blue.
Onion or Rhoeo cells are box-shaped and regularly arranged because of the cell wall, whereas cheek cells are irregularly arranged. Adding 20 per cent sugar solution makes plant cell contents shrink.
Activity 2.4 asks you to study labelled diagrams of a bacterial cell, a plant cell and an animal cell and compare organelles such as the nucleus, chloroplast, mitochondria and cell wall.
Activity 2.5 grows onion roots in water for 5 to 6 days. Root tips are preserved in aceto-alcohol, softened with dilute hydrochloric acid and stained with aceto-carmine to see dividing cells.

problem.en: In Activity 2.1 the field of view is 5 mm across and 25 onion cells fit along the diameter. Estimate one cell.

text.en: Convert the field diameter to micrometres: 5 x 1000 = 5000 micrometres.
Divide by the number of cells: 5000 / 25.
One onion cell is about 200 micrometres long.

why.en: Within the typical range seen in the textbook.

prompt.en: Describe two activities from this chapter and what each shows.

requiredIdeas.en: Potato in water and salt solution shows osmosis
Onion and cheek cells show plant and animal differences
Cell size is field diameter divided by number of cells

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the potato changes weight for no reason

points.en: Cell size can be estimated from the field of view and a cell count.
A potato gains weight in plain water and loses weight in strong salt or sugar solution because of osmosis.
Plant cells are box-shaped with a cell wall; cheek cells are irregular.
Onion root tips show dividing cells when stained.
